then.text: Still warm, that oven. Three days to cool before you can draw the ware. Patience is half of potting.
Look after that Saggit, duck. They're happiest near a warm hearth and a cup of tea, same as me.
Saggars from Middleport, coal off Alf's boat, wad clay from Spode's. You've done the lot! Right, let's fire her.
First the placers go in. They carry the saggars full of ware on their heads, on a little cloth pad, and stack them in columns called bungs, right up into the dome.
Then the wad clay goes between the saggars so no smoke gets in. Then we brick up the doorway. That's the clammins. Daub it with clay. Done.

And now we feed the firemouths, round the clock, for two or three days. I'll pull out trial pieces through a spyhole to see how the ware's coming on. No thermometers in the old days. Just eyes and experience.
Look at her smoke! First firing in this yard in years. The museum's thrilled, the council's furious, and the washing on every line in Longton's gone grey. Proper Potteries.
Here. A firebrick from the oven floor, still warm. And something else was sitting in the ash pit, minding its own business. It's taken a shine to you.
Coal's in. Now some wad clay from the clay cellar at Spode Works, west end of the high street.
Saggars sorted? Grand. Now coal. Boatman Alf's moored on the canal towpath. He'll want paying in some way or other.

else.text: First things first: saggars. Ask for the saggar maker's bottom knocker at Middleport Pottery, by the canal. Yes, that's a real job title.
Ow at, duck? That's 'how are you', round here. I'm the fireman. Not the hose kind. The kiln kind.
These are bottle ovens. Once there were about two thousand of them across the six towns, all puffing away, and you couldn't see the end of your street for smoke.
The museum wants a heritage firing, one day only, smokeless fuel. I've the oven. I've the know-how. What I haven't got is legs like yours.
I need saggars from Middleport Pottery, a load of coal from Boatman Alf on the canal, and wad clay from the clay cellar at Spode's. Fetch them in that order and we'll fire her together.

then.text: That's the last of my coal you'll be getting. Fair fight, mind. Fair fight.
On this cut the boats once carried clay and flint in and crates of china out. Smooth water, fewer breakages. That was Wedgwood's whole idea.
Right you are, a fair fight's a fair fight. Two sacks of coal, best smokeless. Tell the fireman not to waste it.

else.text: Coal for Gladstone? I don't just hand out coal, duck. On the canals you earn your keep. Let's have a scrap first.

then.text: Well, I'll go to the foot of our stairs. Go on, then. Two sacks of coal, best smokeless.

else.text: {greeting} This is the Trent and Mersey. Brindley's canal. North of here it goes through Harecastle Hill in a tunnel over two and a half kilometres long.
The water comes out of that tunnel orange as a satsuma. Iron, from the old mines. The little Rustelvers love it.

then.text: My best delivery lad! Pop inside, the cook's on. And don't forget: an oatcake with cheese is a breakfast, two is a lunch, three is a lifestyle.
All three delivered, still warm? You're a natural, duck.
Here: a dozen oatcakes, a bag of oatmeal, and the recipe. Don't tell anyone in Leek. They think theirs are better. They're wrong.
Last one's for the City fan by the Ground, south of the canal. Cheese and bacon, double.
Next, the landlord at the Leopard, on the high street. Cheese and tomato.

else.text: First stop, the attendant at the Potteries Museum, just along the high street. Plain, with butter.
Ow at, duck? Oatcakes! Hot off the plate! We used to sell them through this window, straight onto the street. Saved on doors.
My delivery lad's off with a cold. I've three orders going cold. Could you run them round? Museum, the Leopard, then the City fan by the Ground.

then.text: Best oatcake I've had since we got promoted. Which I will not say when, as it's a sore point.
Cheese and bacon, double? You beauty. That's matchday sorted.
Stoke City. The Potters. One of the oldest professional clubs there is. And Sir Stanley Matthews played for us. Look at his statue and tell me football's ever been better.

else.text: Red and white stripes, duck. The Potters. We've been playing since the 1860s, and complaining about the referee for about as long.

vale_fan.text: Don't listen to that lot. Port Vale, duck. The Valiants. Burslem's club, the mother town's team.
Two clubs, one city, and a derby where nobody speaks to their own brother-in-law for a week. Lovely.

bennett_fan.text: Arnold Bennett. Born up the road in Hanley, 1867. Went off to London and Paris and got famous writing about here.
He called them the Five Towns. There are six. He thought five sounded better and left Fenton out. Fenton has been cross for over a hundred years.
Read Clayhanger. It's all chimneys and chapel and men in good coats being disappointed. Very relatable.

mitchell_fan.text: Reginald Mitchell. Grew up in Longton, did his apprenticeship at a locomotive works in Fenton, then went off and designed seaplanes.
Then the Spitfire. Those elliptical wings. First flew in 1936. He was ill by then and died the next year, aged forty-two. Never saw what it did.
Go and see the one in the museum. Then tell me engineering isn't art.

paintress.text: {greeting} Forty years I painted pots. Freehand. Bands, sprigs, a little rose, ten thousand times a week.
We were paintresses, the women in the decorating shops. Clarice Cliff started out just like us and ended up with her own range, all bright oranges and jazzy triangles.
Turn a teacup over sometime. If it says Made in England and Stoke on the bottom, somebody like me had their hands on it.

six_towns.text: Tunstall, Burslem, Hanley, Stoke, Fenton, Longton. North to south. Learn them and you'll never get lost, just slightly confused.
Burslem's the mother town, where the potting started. Hanley's the city centre. Stoke has the station and gave the whole lot its name, which the other five find very annoying.

canal_kid.text: Me and me mates fish for Rustelvers off the towpath. You need a long stick and no sense of smell.
Brindley built this canal without proper maps or even writing much down. Did it all in his head, they say. My teacher says that's not an excuse for my homework.

kiln_gran.text: When I were a girl you could count the bottle ovens from our back yard. Hundreds. Smoke so thick you'd hang your washing out white and fetch it in grey.
Then in the fifties they passed the Clean Air Act and the coal firing stopped. Cleaner, mind. You could see the sky. Never knew it was blue.
Have you had lobby? Stew, duck. Meat, spuds, carrots, onions, whatever's left. Staffordshire's answer to everything.

rail_guard.text: Stoke-on-Trent. Change here for anywhere you've been and a fair few places you haven't.
All aboard! Mind the gap, and mind the oatcake crumbs on seat 23.

stoke_bowler.text: The green is round the back, between the beer garden and the bins. Don't tell the brewery we call it a green.
